KEY MESSAGE 1...

Satellite imagery tells two different tales this afternoon, with
the western flank of the forecast area relishing in clear skies
and sunshine while the eastern half remains entrenched beneath 
low stratus. A cold front that passed through earlier today has 
since completed its passage through the area, leaving behind 
leftover clouds and embedded light rain and drizzle. Additional 
clearing is progged to prosper over the next few hours in the 
lowlands, while clouds remain intact along the higher terrain 
until late tonight.

Surface high pressure settles into the area for the next two
days, advertising dry, albeit cooler, air. Forecast soundings
for today showed a completely moist thermal profile amid the
frontal passage earlier then transforming into a very dry
atmospheric column by this evening. This should mitigate river
valley fog for the bulk of the area tonight outside of the
higher elevations. Otherwise, a surge of colder air filters in
beginning overnight, leading to Tuesday morning lows bottoming
out into the 20s/low 30s. 

A slight moderating in daytime temperatures are progged from
Tuesday into Wednesday, returning to their climatological norms
for this time of year for the majority of our climate sites.
While sunny to start the day Wednesday, clouds will invade from
the south by the afternoon ahead of the next system, messaged in
more detail below.


KEY MESSAGE 2...

Heading into Wednesday, two areas of low pressure will be in 
contention to impose hazardous travel conditions for the 
Thanksgiving holiday and into the end of the week. The first
area of note will originate off the coast of Texas while the
second is progged to be churning along the Florida and Carolina
coastlines. An upper level low positioned over the Central
Plains will spin these two surface features northward and
merging them into one large area of low pressure beginning as
early as late Wednesday evening. This system is progged to
stretch from Chicago and eastward towards the Delmarva coast on
Thursday before slowly spinning into New England for the start 
of the weekend.

How this shapes up for the forecast area remains generally the
same as previous thinking heading into the holiday timeframe.
Above freezing temperatures at the onset of showers invading
from the south will infer widespread rain to start off this
event. Moderate to heavy rain masks the entire area Thursday
morning before lessening in coverage through the day as the bulk
of the system lifts northward. However, this nearly stacked 
system looks to be at its strongest late Thursday night into 
Friday, with additional aide from colder air that will promote a
transition over to a wintry mix of precipitation, followed by a
full transformation to snow along our mountain zones on Friday.
While we remain out of time range for forecast snowfall
accumulations, central guidance and various global models depict
light amounts of snow could gradually culminate into a few
inches as lake enhanced showers extend their stay into the
weekend.

Additionally, a tightened pressure gradient attached to this
strong system will yield gusty to strong winds across the area
from late Wednesday night into the weekend. Peak forecast gusts
nearing advisory thresholds were noted along the spine of the
Appalachians, while the lowlands and surrounding foothills could
see gusts as strong as 20 to 30 miles per hour through the
course of this event.

Hazardous travel during this upcoming holiday could come in two
forms. One being the wet roadways prompted by the heavy rain and
plentiful runoff likely to arise as a result. Areas could
receive a few inches of rainfall from Thursday into Friday,
contributing to upticks in local creek and stream flooding
potential. This could also become the case for blocked culverts
on local streets in response to leaf debris. The secondary area
of concern for hazards will be along the mountains with the
combination of wintry precipitation and strong, gusty winds. 

A return to drier, quieter weather is currently slated by the
balance of the weekend.
